cells.tense: Time with the thing is time well spent right now.
cells.ask: Keep one daily session this week and note what it opens onto, not just what it improves.
cells.core:
You've found a piece of work you can sit down to without dragging yourself there. The repetitions hold because you choose them, and they don't cost you the rest of your life — you come back from the quiet a little more present with people, not less.

What you're building is skill, not a case against yourself. Somewhere in the repetitions you've started to see how it works underneath — the shape of the thing once the details fall away. That's the part this reading is for. The practice is a lens, and it's still clear. When a day gets missed or a stretch goes flat, nothing about that tells you the work has stopped being yours.
cells.sheetLine: The practice is steady, and it's still opening the thing up.
cells.verb: keeping one small thing lit by returning to it again and again
cells.place: where the pattern shows itself once the details fall away

cells.tense: You're aiming at a finished version that keeps moving further out.
cells.ask: Stop one session at a clear stopping point while it's still imperfect, on purpose.
cells.core:
The hours have started guarding the door. What was solitude by choice now feels like the only safe place to work — and the refinement keeps promising that one more pass will finally make it right. That promise doesn't come due, so the passes keep going.

You already see the pattern underneath; that's why the flaws stand out so sharply. But seeing a mechanism this clearly doesn't oblige you to scrub every surface of it. Some of what you're grinding down is finished. Leaving a session at a clear stopping point while it's still imperfect would tell you you can put the work down and come back to people without losing it — and that the work holds while you're away from it.
cells.sheetLine: You're refining past the point of finished. The work can survive a pause.

cells.tense: The thing you practiced back then stopped arriving here a long time ago.
cells.ask: Do ten minutes of the old practice tomorrow, then leave it alone until the next day.
cells.core:
There's a kind of regular work you don't get near anymore. Nothing here explains that, and it doesn't need explaining to read it — when the time comes to sit down with the thing, something in the body says no.

Meanwhile the pattern-reading still runs. You notice how things work underneath, clearly, and you'd rather use that than be seen doing the slow version. But seeing a mechanism and having your hands on it are different. Ten minutes of the old practice, then leaving it until tomorrow, keeps the showing small enough to make. You get to be someone who does this, in whatever amount the day allows — and the amount you set is the amount that counts.
cells.sheetLine: Ten minutes of practice, no more, is still the practice.

cells.tense: The skill is already built. You still call it something that happens to you.
cells.ask: The next time someone asks how you do it, describe one step you take rather than calling it instinct.
cells.core:
You can see the pattern underneath, and you're already good at the practice that produced that sight — the repetitions just don't get counted as yours. When people ask how you do it, "I just can" is the answer. But someone watched and kept at it. That someone is doing the work right now.

The doing runs on its own; the saying-so hasn't caught up. You don't have to call yourself an expert, and you don't have to enjoy it. Just try naming, once, what the steps actually are — the thing you check, the order you do it in, the part you keep doing even when it stops being interesting. Naming one step doesn't close the question of who did this. It just puts your name on a thing that already has it.
cells.sheetLine: You did the reps. Say so, one step at a time.
